result.statement: If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the greater segment added to the half of the whole is five times the square on the half.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, AC being the greater segment. Bisect AB at E [1.10], so that AE = EB. Produce BA beyond A [P2], and on the produced part cut off AD equal to AE [1.3]. Then AD = AE = EB, so AD is the half of the whole AB. The points D, A, C, B lie in this order on one straight line; hence DC is a straight line cut at A into the segments DA, AC, and AB is a straight line cut at E into the equal segments AE, EB. We must show that the square on DC (the greater segment AC together with the half AD) is five times the square on AD.

**Step 2.** Since AB is cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, AC being the greater segment, by D6.3, as AB is to AC, so is AC to CB.

**Step 3.** Thus the three straight lines AB, AC, CB are proportional, so by 6.17 the rectangle contained by the extremes is equal to the square on the mean: rect(AB, CB) = sq(AC).

**Step 4.** Since AB is cut at C, by 2.2 the rectangles contained by the whole and each segment together equal the square on the whole: rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB) = sq(AB). By Step 3, rect(AB, CB) = sq(AC); adding rect(AB, AC) to these equals [CN2], rect(AB, AC) + sq(AC) = rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB), and therefore [CN1] rect(AB, AC) + sq(AC) = sq(AB).

**Step 5.** Since DC is cut at A, by 2.4 the square on the whole equals the squares on the segments together with twice the rectangle contained by the segments: sq(DC) = sq(DA) + sq(AC) + 2 rect(DA, AC).

**Step 6.** Since AB is cut at E into AE, EB, by 2.1 the rectangle contained by AC and AB equals the rectangles contained by AC and each segment: rect(AC, AB) = rect(AC, AE) + rect(AC, EB). By D2.1 a rectangle is contained, and so determined, by the two straight lines about its right angle; since AE and EB are each equal to AD, rect(AC, AE) = rect(AC, AD) and rect(AC, EB) = rect(AC, AD). Hence [CN2, CN1] rect(AB, AC) = 2 rect(DA, AC).

**Step 7.** Since AB is cut at E, by 2.4 sq(AB) = sq(AE) + sq(EB) + 2 rect(AE, EB). Because AE = EB, the rectangle contained by AE, EB is equilateral as well as right-angled, that is, it is the square on AE [D1.22]; and because AE and EB are each equal to AD, the squares on AE and on EB are each equal to the square on AD. Therefore [CN2] sq(AB) = sq(AD) + sq(AD) + 2 sq(AD) = 4 sq(AD).

**Step 8.** Combining these results: sq(DC) = sq(AD) + sq(AC) + 2 rect(DA, AC) [Step 5] = sq(AD) + sq(AC) + rect(AB, AC) [Step 6, CN2] = sq(AD) + sq(AB) [Step 4, CN2] = sq(AD) + 4 sq(AD) [Step 7, CN2] = 5 sq(AD).

**Step 9.** Therefore the square on DC, which is the greater segment AC added to the half AD of the whole, is five times the square on the half AD. This is what was to be proved.

Path note: the identity sq(DC) = sq(AB) + sq(AD) was obtained directly from the Book II area propositions (2.1, 2.2, 2.4) rather than by describing squares and comparing gnomons; the Book II route is the more direct.

result.statement: If the square on a straight line be five times the square on a segment of it, then, when the double of the said segment is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is the remaining part of the original straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line and C a point on it, so that AC is a segment of AB and CB the remaining part, and let the square on AB be five times the square on AC. Produce AB beyond B (P2). On the straight line so produced, cut off from C, in the direction of B, CE equal to AC, and from E, in the same direction, ED equal to AC (1.3). Then CD is double of AC, E is the middle point of CD, and D lies on the line on the same side of C as B. I say that, when CD is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is CB.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB (2.4).

**Step 3.** By hypothesis the square on AB is five times the square on AC, that is, four times the square on AC together with the square on AC. Therefore the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB are equal to four times the square on AC together with the square on AC (CN1). Subtracting the square on AC from each, the square on CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB is equal to four times the square on AC (CN3).

**Step 4.** Since CD is cut at E, the square on CD is equal to the squares on CE, ED together with twice the rectangle contained by CE, ED (2.4). But CE and ED are each equal to AC, so each of the squares on CE, ED and the rectangle CE, ED is equal to the square on AC; hence the square on CD is four times the square on AC. Therefore the square on CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB is equal to the square on CD (CN1).

**Step 5.** Since CD is cut at E, the rectangle contained by CB, CD is equal to the rectangles contained by CB, CE and by CB, ED (2.1); and since CE, ED are each equal to AC, each of these rectangles is equal to the rectangle AC, CB. Therefore the rectangle CD, CB is twice the rectangle AC, CB, and so, by Step 4, the square on CB together with the rectangle CD, CB is equal to the square on CD (CN1).

**Step 6.** I say that CB is less than CD. For, if not, CB is either equal to or greater than CD. If CB is equal to CD, the square on CB is equal to the square on CD. If CB is greater than CD, cut off from CB the part CF equal to CD (1.3); then the square on CB is equal to the squares on CF, FB together with twice the rectangle CF, FB (2.4), so that the square on CB is greater than the square on CF, that is, than the square on CD (CN5). In either case the square on CB is not less than the square on CD; hence the square on CB together with the rectangle CD, CB is greater than the square on CD (CN5). But by Step 5 it is equal to the square on CD: which is impossible. Therefore CB is less than CD; and since B and D lie on the same side of C, the point B lies between C and D, so that CD is cut at B into the segments CB, BD.

**Step 7.** Since CD is cut at B, the rectangle contained by CD, CB together with the rectangle contained by CD, BD is equal to the square on CD (2.2).

**Step 8.** Therefore, by Steps 5 and 7, the square on CB together with the rectangle CD, CB is equal to the rectangle CD, CB together with the rectangle CD, BD (CN1). Subtracting the rectangle CD, CB from each, the square on CB is equal to the rectangle contained by CD, BD (CN3).

**Step 9.** Since the rectangle contained by the extremes CD, BD is equal to the square on the mean CB, the three straight lines CD, CB, BD are proportional: as CD is to CB, so is CB to BD (6.17).

**Step 10.** Since CB is a part of CD, CD is greater than CB (CN5). And in the proportion CD : CB = CB : BD the first term CD is greater than the third term CB; therefore the second term CB is greater than the fourth term BD (5.14).

**Step 11.** Therefore the straight line CD, which is double of the segment AC, is so cut at B that, as the whole CD is to the greater segment CB, so is CB to the less segment BD; that is, CD is cut in extreme and mean ratio at B (D6.3), and its greater segment CB is the remaining part of the original straight line AB. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the lesser segment added to the half of the greater segment is five times the square on the half of the greater segment.
result.proof:
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the lesser segment added to the half of the greater segment is five times the square on the half of the greater segment.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio at the point C, and let AC be the greater segment, so that CB is the lesser segment. Bisect AC at the point D [1.10]; then AD = DC. We must show that the square on DB (the lesser segment CB together with the half DC of the greater segment) is five times the square on DC.

**Step 2.** Since AB is cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, as AB is to AC, so is AC to CB [D6.3].

**Step 3.** Since the three straight lines AB, AC, CB are proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes AB, CB is equal to the square on the mean AC [6.17]; that is, rect(AB, BC) = sq(AC).

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AC is cut at random at D, the square on AC is equal to the squares on AD, DC together with twice the rectangle contained by AD, DC [2.4]. But AD = DC (Step 1); hence the square on AD is equal to the square on DC, and the rectangle contained by AD, DC, being right-angled and having its adjacent sides AD, DC equal, is a square, namely the square on DC [D1.22]. Therefore the square on AC is equal to four times the square on DC.

**Step 5.** Since C lies on AB and D lies on AC, the points D, C, B lie in a straight line, and CB is added in a straight line to AC, which is bisected at D. Therefore, by [2.6], the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line and the added straight line, together with the square on the half, is equal to the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line: rect(AB, BC) + sq(DC) = sq(DB).

**Step 6.** But rect(AB, BC) = sq(AC) (Step 3), and sq(AC) = 4·sq(DC) (Step 4); therefore rect(AB, BC) = 4·sq(DC) [CN1].

**Step 7.** Substituting in Step 5, sq(DB) = 4·sq(DC) + sq(DC) = 5·sq(DC) [CN2].

**Step 8.** Therefore the square on DB, which is the lesser segment CB added to the half DC of the greater segment AC, is five times the square on DC, the half of the greater segment. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 1.10, D6.3, 6.17, 2.4, D1.22, 2.6, CN1, CN2

result.statement: If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the whole and the square on the lesser segment together are triple of the square on the greater segment.
result.proof:
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the whole and the square on the lesser segment together are triple of the square on the greater segment.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio at the point C, and let AC be the greater segment. Then by the definition of extreme and mean ratio (D6.3), as the whole AB is to the greater segment AC, so is AC to the lesser segment CB; that is, AB : AC = AC : CB.

**Step 2.** Since the three straight lines AB, AC, CB are proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes AB, CB is equal to the square on the mean AC (6.17). Thus rect(AB, CB) = sq(AC).

**Step 3.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment CB is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments AC, CB together with the square on CB (2.3). Thus rect(AB, CB) = rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB).

**Step 4.** From Steps 2 and 3, since rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB) and sq(AC) are each equal to rect(AB, CB), they are equal to one another (CN1). Thus rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB) = sq(AC).

**Step 5.** Again, since AB is cut at C, the square on the whole AB is equal to the squares on the segments AC, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB (2.4). Thus sq(AB) = sq(AC) + sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB).

**Step 6.** Add the square on CB to both sides of the equality in Step 5 (CN2). Then sq(AB) + sq(CB) = sq(AC) + 2·sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB) = sq(AC) + 2·[rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB)].

**Step 7.** But by Step 4, rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB) = sq(AC), so twice that sum is twice the square on AC, i.e. 2·[rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB)] = 2·sq(AC) (CN2). Substituting into Step 6 (CN1), sq(AB) + sq(CB) = sq(AC) + 2·sq(AC) = 3·sq(AC).

**Step 8.** Therefore the square on the whole AB and the square on the lesser segment CB together are triple of the square on the greater segment AC. Q.E.D.

**Path note:** Instead of constructing the square on AB (1.46) and arguing through the gnomon, the proof proceeds directly through the identities of 2.3 and 2.4 combined with 6.17; this is the most direct route and avoids any auxiliary figure.

**USED:** D6.3, 6.17, 2.3, 2.4, CN1, CN2

result.statement: If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, and there be added to it a straight line equal to the greater segment, the whole straight line has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and the original straight line is the greater segment.
result.proof:
## Proposition 13.5
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, and there be added to it a straight line equal to the greater segment, the whole straight line has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and the original straight line is the greater segment.

Let the straight line AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio at the point C, AC being the greater segment, and let the straight line AD, equal to AC, be added to AB at the end A, so that D, A, B lie in one straight line with A between D and B. I say that DB has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at A, and that the original straight line AB is the greater segment.

**Step 1.** Since AB has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, and AC is the greater segment, by the definition of extreme and mean ratio, as the whole AB is to the greater segment AC, so is AC to the lesser segment CB [D6.3].

**Step 2.** Therefore, inversely, as AC is to AB, so is CB to AC [5.7, Porism].

**Step 3.** Since AD is equal to AC, the equal magnitudes AD and AC have the same ratio to the same magnitude AB; therefore, as AD is to AB, so is AC to AB [5.7]. But as AC is to AB, so is CB to AC (Step 2); therefore, as AD is to AB, so is CB to AC [5.11].

**Step 4.** The magnitudes AD, AB, CB, AC are thus proportional separando; therefore they are also proportional componendo: as AD together with AB is to AB, so is CB together with AC to AC [5.18]. Now AD together with AB is the whole DB, since A lies between D and B; and CB together with AC is the whole AB, since C lies between A and B. Therefore, as DB is to AB, so is AB to AC.

**Step 5.** Again, since AC is equal to AD, the same magnitude AB has the same ratio to the equal magnitudes AC and AD; therefore, as AB is to AC, so is AB to AD [5.7]. But as DB is to AB, so is AB to AC (Step 4); therefore, as DB is to AB, so is AB to AD [5.11].

**Step 6.** Now DB is greater than AB, for the whole is greater than the part [CN5]. And since the first DB has to the second AB the same ratio as the third AB has to the fourth AD, and the first DB is greater than the third AB, the second AB is also greater than the fourth AD [5.14].

**Step 7.** Therefore the straight line DB has been cut at A so that, as the whole DB is to the greater segment AB, so is the greater segment AB to the lesser segment AD. Hence DB has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at A [D6.3], and the original straight line AB is the greater segment. Q.E.D.

**USED:** D6.3, 5.7, 5.11, 5.18, CN5, 5.14

*Path note:* An alternative route exists through areas — converting the hypothesis to rect(AB, BC) = sq(AC) by 6.17, showing rect(DB, DA) = sq(AB) by 2.3 and 2.2, and converting back by 6.17. The proportional route above is chosen because D6.3 is itself stated as a proportion and the conclusion follows from two Book 5 manipulations (inversion and componendo) without passing through areas.

result.statement: If a rational straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, each of the segments is the irrational straight line called apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a rational straight line cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, with AC the greater segment, so that, as AB is to AC, so is AC to CB (D6.3). It is to be proved that each of the segments AC, CB is the irrational straight line called apotome.

**Step 2.** Produce BA beyond A (P2). Bisect AB at M (1.10), and from the produced line cut off AD equal to AM, the half of AB (1.3). Then D, A, C, B lie in this order on one straight line, DA is half of AB, and DC is made up of DA together with the greater segment AC.

**Step 3.** Since AB has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, and AD, the half of the whole AB, has been added to the greater segment AC, the square on CD is five times the square on DA (13.1).

**Step 4.** Hence the square on CD has to the square on DA the ratio which the number 5 has to the unit, that is, the ratio which a number has to a number; therefore the square on CD is commensurable with the square on DA (10.6).

**Step 5.** Since AB is double of DA, AB has to DA the ratio which the number 2 has to the unit; therefore DA is commensurable in length with AB (10.6). But AB is rational; therefore DA is also rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 6.** Since DA is commensurable in length with AB, the square on DA has to the square on AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9); therefore the square on DA is commensurable with the square on AB (10.6). But the square on the rational straight line AB is a rational area; therefore the square on DA is also rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 7.** Now the square on CD is commensurable with the square on DA (Step 4), and the square on DA is commensurable with the square on AB (Step 6); therefore the square on CD is commensurable with the square on AB (10.12). Hence the square on CD is rational (D10.1.4); and CD, being commensurable in square with the rational straight line AB (D10.1.2), is itself rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 8.** But 5 to 1 is not the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore the square on CD has not to the square on DA the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and so CD is incommensurable in length with DA (10.9).

**Step 9.** Therefore CD, DA are rational straight lines (Steps 5, 7) which are commensurable in square, since their squares are commensurable (Step 4, D10.1.2), but not in length (Step 8); that is, they are commensurable in square only. Thus from the rational straight line CD there has been subtracted the rational straight line DA, which is commensurable with the whole CD in square only; therefore the remainder CA is an apotome (10.73).

**Step 10.** Again, since, as AB is to AC, so is AC to CB (Step 1), the three straight lines AB, AC, CB are proportional; therefore the rectangle contained by the extremes AB, BC is equal to the square on the mean AC (6.17).

**Step 11.** Thus the square on the apotome AC, when applied to the rational straight line AB, produces BC as breadth. But the square on an apotome, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a first apotome (10.97). Therefore CB is a first apotome, and hence CB is an apotome (D10.3.1).

**Step 12.** Therefore, AB being a rational straight line cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, the greater segment AC is an apotome (Step 9) and the lesser segment CB is an apotome (Step 11); that is, each of the segments is the irrational straight line called apotome. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If three angles of an equilateral pentagon, taken either in order or not in order, be equal, the pentagon will be equiangular.
result.proof:
**Statement.** If three angles of an equilateral pentagon, taken either in order or not in order, be equal, the pentagon will be equiangular.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be an equilateral pentagon, so that AB = BC = CD = DE = EA. As for all of Euclid's pentagons it is convex, so a diagonal drawn from a vertex falls within the angle of the pentagon at that vertex; this is what allows two angles at a vertex to be added to give the angle of the pentagon there. Three of the five angles are either three consecutive angles, which we may label as those at A, B, C, or two consecutive angles together with the one not adjacent to either, which we may label as those at A, B, D. We treat the two cases in turn.

**Step 2.** First case: the angles at A, B, C, taken in order, are equal, so ∠EAB = ∠ABC = ∠BCD. Join AC, BD and AD [P1].

**Step 3.** In the triangles ABC, DCB the side AB equals the side DC, the side BC is common, and the included angle ∠ABC equals the included angle ∠DCB (given). Therefore the base AC equals the base DB [1.4].

**Step 4.** In the triangles ACD, DBA the two sides CD, DA are equal to the two sides BA, AD respectively (CD = BA, and DA is common), and the base AC equals the base DB (Step 3). Therefore the angles contained by the equal sides are equal: ∠CDA = ∠BAD [1.8].

**Step 5.** In the triangle EAD the sides EA, ED are equal; therefore the angles at the base are equal, ∠EDA = ∠EAD [1.5].

**Step 6.** Adding the equals of Step 4 to the equals of Step 5 [CN2]: ∠CDA + ∠ADE = ∠BAD + ∠DAE. Since DA falls within ∠CDE and AD falls within ∠BAE, this says ∠CDE = ∠BAE. Hence the angle at D equals the angle at A.

**Step 7.** Join BE and CE [P1]. In the triangles EAB, CBA the side EA equals the side CB, the side AB is common, and the included angle ∠EAB equals the included angle ∠CBA (given). Therefore the base EB equals the base CA [1.4].

**Step 8.** In the triangles EBC, CAE the two sides BC, CE are equal to the two sides AE, EC respectively (BC = AE, and CE is common), and the base EB equals the base CA (Step 7). Therefore the angles contained by the equal sides are equal: ∠BCE = ∠AEC [1.8].

**Step 9.** In the triangle DCE the sides DC, DE are equal; therefore ∠DCE = ∠DEC [1.5].

**Step 10.** Adding the equals of Step 8 to the equals of Step 9 [CN2]: ∠BCE + ∠ECD = ∠AEC + ∠CED. Since CE falls within ∠BCD and EC falls within ∠AED, this says ∠BCD = ∠AED. Hence the angle at E equals the angle at C.

**Step 11.** The angles at A, B, C are equal by hypothesis, the angle at D equals the angle at A (Step 6), and the angle at E equals the angle at C (Step 10). Therefore all five angles are equal to one another [CN1], and the pentagon ABCDE is equiangular. This completes the first case.

**Step 12.** Second case: the angles at A, B, D, not taken in order, are equal, so ∠EAB = ∠ABC = ∠CDE. Join EB and EC [P1].

**Step 13.** In the triangles EAB, EDC the side EA equals the side ED, the side AB equals the side DC, and the included angle ∠EAB equals the included angle ∠EDC (given). Therefore the base EB equals the base EC, and the remaining angles equal the remaining angles opposite the equal sides; in particular ∠EBA = ∠ECD [1.4].

**Step 14.** In the triangle EBC the sides EB, EC are equal (Step 13); therefore ∠EBC = ∠ECB [1.5].

**Step 15.** Adding the equals of Step 13 to the equals of Step 14 [CN2]: ∠ABE + ∠EBC = ∠DCE + ∠ECB. Since BE falls within ∠ABC and CE falls within ∠BCD, this says ∠ABC = ∠BCD. Hence the angle at C equals the angle at B, and since the angle at B equals the angle at A, the angle at C also equals the angle at A [CN1].

**Step 16.** Thus in the second case the three angles at A, B, C, taken in order, are equal, and by the first case (Steps 2–11) the pentagon is equiangular. Therefore, whether the three equal angles are taken in order or not in order, the equilateral pentagon is equiangular. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, CN1, CN2, 1.4, 1.5, 1.8

result.statement: If in an equilateral and equiangular pentagon straight lines subtend two angles taken in order, they cut one another in extreme and mean ratio, and their greater segments are equal to the side of the pentagon.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the equilateral and equiangular pentagon. Join AC and BE [P1]; AC subtends the angle ABC and BE subtends the angle BAE, two angles of the pentagon taken in order. Let AC and BE cut one another at H, so that H lies between B and E on BE and between A and C on AC. It is to be proved that BE and AC are each cut at H in extreme and mean ratio, and that their greater segments are equal to the side of the pentagon.

**Step 2.** In the triangles EAB and ABC, EA = AB and AB = BC, since the pentagon is equilateral, and the angle EAB = the angle ABC, since the pentagon is equiangular. Therefore the base EB = the base AC, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles which the equal sides subtend: the angle AEB = the angle BAC, and the angle ABE = the angle BCA [1.4].

**Step 3.** In the triangle EAB, since EA = AB, the angle AEB = the angle ABE [1.5]. Combining with Step 2, the angle ABE = the angle AEB = the angle BAC [CN1]. Since H lies on BE and on AC, this says that the angle HBA = the angle HAB.

**Step 4.** In the triangle ABH the side BH is produced to E; hence the exterior angle AHE is equal to the two interior and opposite angles HAB and HBA taken together [1.32]. By Step 3 each of these is equal to the angle BAC, so the angle AHE is equal to the sum of two angles each equal to the angle BAC [CN2].

**Step 5.** Circumscribe the circle ABCDE about the pentagon [4.14]. Since the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA fitted into this circle are equal, they cut off equal circumferences AB, BC, CD, DE, EA [3.28].

**Step 6.** Join AD [P1]. The angles BAC, CAD, DAE at the circumference stand respectively on the equal circumferences BC, CD, DE; therefore the angle BAC = the angle CAD = the angle DAE [3.27]. Since D lies on the circumference CDE, the straight line AD falls within the angle CAE, so that the angle CAE is the sum of the angles CAD and DAE, that is, the sum of two angles each equal to the angle BAC [CN2]. Hence, by Step 4, the angle HAE (which is the angle CAE) is equal to the angle AHE [CN1].

**Step 7.** In the triangle AHE the angle AHE = the angle HAE; therefore the sides subtending these equal angles are equal, namely EA = EH [1.6]. But EA = AB, being a side of the pentagon; therefore EH = AB, the side of the pentagon [CN1].

**Step 8.** Consider the triangles EBA and ABH. The angle EBA is common to both, since the angle ABH is the same angle. The angle BEA = the angle BAC (Step 2) = the angle BAH, since H lies on AC. Therefore the remaining angle BAE of the triangle EBA is equal to the remaining angle BHA of the triangle ABH, each being what remains when two equal sums are taken from two right angles [1.32, CN3]. The triangles EBA and ABH are therefore equiangular, and the sides about the equal angles are proportional, the corresponding sides being those which subtend the equal angles: as EB is to BA, so is AB to BH [6.4] (EB and AB subtend the equal angles BAE, BHA; BA and BH subtend the equal angles BEA, BAH).

**Step 9.** Since BA = EH (Step 7), EB has to BA the same ratio as EB has to EH, and AB has to BH the same ratio as EH has to HB [5.7]. Therefore, as EB is to EH, so is EH to HB [5.11].

**Step 10.** EB is greater than its part EH [CN5]. In the proportion EB : EH = EH : HB the first magnitude EB is greater than the third EH; therefore the second EH is greater than the fourth HB [5.14]. Thus the whole BE is to its greater segment EH as EH is to the lesser segment HB; that is, BE has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at H [D6.3], and its greater segment EH is equal to the side of the pentagon (Step 7).

**Step 11.** Now for AC. In the triangle ABH the angle HAB = the angle HBA (Step 3); therefore HA = HB [1.6]. Also AC = EB (Step 2). Subtracting the equals HA, HB from the equals AC, EB, the remainders are equal: HC = HE [CN3]. Hence HC = HE = AB, the side of the pentagon [CN1].

**Step 12.** Since AC = EB and HC = EH, AC has to HC the same ratio as EB has to HC, and EB has to HC the same ratio as EB has to EH [5.7]; therefore AC : HC = EB : EH [5.11]. Likewise, since EH = HC and HB = HA, EH : HB = HC : HA [5.7, 5.11]. But EB : EH = EH : HB (Step 9); therefore AC : HC = HC : HA [5.11]. AC is greater than its part HC [CN5], so HC is greater than HA [5.14]. Therefore AC has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at H [D6.3], and its greater segment HC is equal to the side of the pentagon (Step 11).

**Step 13.** Therefore the straight lines AC, BE, which subtend two angles of the equilateral and equiangular pentagon taken in order, cut one another at H in extreme and mean ratio, and their greater segments EH, HC are each equal to the side of the pentagon. Q.E.D.

Path note: the doubling of the angle BAC in Step 6 could alternatively be obtained from the proportionality of angles at the circumference to the arcs they stand on, without joining AD; the equal-arc route was chosen as the more elementary.

result.statement: If the side of the hexagon and that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle be added together, the whole straight line has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and its greater segment is the side of the hexagon.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle; let BC be the side of the equilateral decagon inscribed in it and CD the side of the hexagon inscribed in the same circle, and let BC and CD be placed in a straight line, so that BCD is one straight line. I say that BD is cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, and that CD is its greater segment.

**Step 2.** Take the centre E of the circle [3.1]; join EB, EC, ED [P1]; and produce BE beyond E to meet the circumference again at A [P2]. Since E is the centre, EA = EB = EC [D1.15].

**Step 3.** BA passes through the centre and is terminated at both ends by the circumference; it is therefore a diameter and bisects the circle [D1.17], so the circumference ACB is half of the whole circumference. Since the ten equal sides of the inscribed decagon cut off ten equal circumferences [3.28], the whole circumference is ten times the circumference BC; hence the circumference ACB is five times the circumference BC. Taking away the circumference BC from the circumference ACB, the remaining circumference AC is four times the circumference CB [CN3].

**Step 4.** The angles AEC and CEB at the centre stand on the circumferences AC and CB respectively, and angles in the same circle have the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand [6.33]; therefore, since circumference AC is four times circumference CB, angle AEC is four times angle CEB.

**Step 5.** In triangle EBC, EB = EC, so angle ECB = angle EBC [1.5]. Since BE is produced to A, angle AEC is the exterior angle of triangle EBC at E, and equals the sum of the two interior and opposite angles EBC and ECB [1.32]; therefore angle AEC is double angle ECB.

**Step 6.** CD is the side of the hexagon inscribed in the circle, and the side of the inscribed hexagon equals the radius of the circle [4.15]; so CD = EC [CN1]. Hence in triangle ECD, angle CED = angle CDE [1.5]. Since DC is produced to B (BCD being a straight line), angle ECB is the exterior angle of triangle ECD at C, and equals the sum of the interior and opposite angles CED and CDE [1.32]; therefore angle ECB is double angle EDC.

**Step 7.** Angle AEC is double angle ECB (Step 5) and angle ECB is double angle EDC (Step 6); therefore angle AEC is four times angle EDC. But angle AEC is also four times angle CEB (Step 4). Hence four times angle CEB equals four times angle EDC [CN1], and so angle EDC = angle CEB.

**Step 8.** Consider triangles EBD and EBC. The angle at B is common to both (angle EBD is the same angle as angle EBC, since C lies on BD), and angle EDB = angle BEC (Step 7). Since the three angles of every triangle are together equal to two right angles [1.32], the remaining angle BED of triangle EBD equals the remaining angle ECB of triangle EBC. Therefore triangle EBD is equiangular with triangle EBC.

**Step 9.** In equiangular triangles the sides about the equal angles are proportional, those which subtend the equal angles being corresponding [6.4]. The side DB subtends angle BED and the side EB subtends the equal angle ECB; the side BE subtends angle EDB and the side BC subtends the equal angle BEC. Therefore DB : BE = EB : BC.

**Step 10.** Now BE = CD, both being equal to the radius EC (Steps 2 and 6). Equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude, and the same magnitude has the same ratio to equal magnitudes [5.7]; so DB : BE = DB : CD and EB : BC = CD : BC. Ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another [5.11]; therefore BD : DC = DC : CB.

**Step 11.** BD is greater than its part DC [CN5]. In the proportion BD : DC = DC : CB the first term BD exceeds the third term DC; therefore the second term DC exceeds the fourth term CB [5.14]. Thus DC is the greater and CB the lesser segment of BD.

**Step 12.** As the whole BD is to its greater segment DC, so is the greater segment DC to the lesser segment CB; therefore BD has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at C [D6.3], and its greater segment DC is the side of the hexagon. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the circle and ABCDE the equilateral pentagon inscribed in it. Take the centre F of the circle (3.1). Join AF and produce it to meet the circumference at G; join FB (P1, P2). From F draw FH perpendicular to AB (1.12) and produce FH beyond H to meet the circumference at K (P2); join AK, KB (P1). From F draw FL perpendicular to AK (1.12) and produce FL beyond L to meet the circumference at M (P2); let N be the point in which FM cuts AB (F and M lie on opposite sides of AB), and join KN (P1).

**Step 2.** Since the pentagon is equilateral, its equal sides cut off equal arcs: arc AB = arc BC = arc CD = arc DE = arc EA (3.28). These five equal arcs together make up the whole circumference, so each is a fifth part of it. Arc ABC, being two of these five parts, is less than a semicircumference, so G, the other end of the diameter AG, lies on arc CD; likewise K lies on arc AB and M on arc AK.

**Step 3.** Since AG is a diameter, it bisects the circle (D1.17); therefore the arc ABCG is equal to the arc AEDG. Of these, arc ABC (arcs AB, BC together) is equal to arc AED (arcs AE, ED together), each being made up of two of the equal arcs (CN2). Subtracting these from the equal semicircumferences, the remaining arc CG is equal to the remaining arc GD (CN3). Hence arc CD is double arc CG.

**Step 4.** The straight line FK passes through the centre and cuts AB, which does not pass through the centre, at right angles; therefore it bisects AB, so that AH = HB (3.3). In the triangles AFH, BFH the two sides AH, HF are equal to the two sides BH, HF respectively, and the angle AHF is equal to the angle BHF, these being the equal adjacent angles made by the perpendicular FH on AB (D1.10); therefore angle AFH = angle BFH (1.4). These equal angles at the centre stand on the arcs AK, KB; therefore arc AK = arc KB (3.26). Hence arc AB is double arc BK, and arc AK, being half of the fifth part AB, is a tenth part of the circumference.

**Step 5.** In the same way FM passes through the centre and cuts AK at right angles at L, so that AL = LK (3.3). The triangles AFL, KFL have AL = LK, FL common, and the angle ALF equal to the angle KLF (D1.10); therefore angle AFL = angle KFL (1.4), whence arc AM = arc MK (3.26). Hence arc AK is double arc KM, and therefore arc BK, which equals arc AK, is also double arc KM.

**Step 6.** Arc CD is equal to arc AB (Step 2); arc CD is double arc CG (Step 3) and arc AB is double arc BK (Step 4); therefore arc CG, the half of arc CD, is equal to arc BK, the half of arc AB. Hence arc CG is double arc KM (Step 5). Again, arc CB is equal to arc AB, which is double arc BK. Adding, the whole arc GB (arc GC together with arc CB) is double the arc made up of KM and KB, that is, double arc BM (CN2).

**Step 7.** In the same circle, angles at the centre have the same ratio as the arcs on which they stand (6.33); and arc GB is double arc BM; therefore the angle GFB is double the angle BFM.

**Step 8.** Since AF is produced to G, the angle GFB is the exterior angle of the triangle AFB and is equal to the two interior and opposite angles FAB, FBA (1.32); and since FA = FB, angle FAB = angle FBA (1.5); therefore angle GFB is double angle FAB. Thus the double of angle BFM and the double of angle FAB are each equal to angle GFB, and so are equal to one another (CN1); therefore angle BFM = angle FAB. Since N lies on FM, this says angle BFN = angle FAB.

**Step 9.** In the triangles ABF, FBN the angle ABF is common (N lying on BA), and the angle BAF is equal to the angle BFN; therefore the remaining angle AFB is equal to the remaining angle FNB (1.32), and the triangles are equiangular. Hence the sides about the equal angles are proportional, the sides subtending equal angles corresponding: AB : BF = FB : BN (6.4). Since the three straight lines AB, BF, BN are proportional, the rectangle contained by AB, BN is equal to the square on BF (6.17).

**Step 10.** In the triangles ALN, KLN, AL = LK (Step 5), LN is common, and the angles ALN, KLN are equal, being the equal adjacent angles made by the perpendicular FL on AK (D1.10); therefore the angle LAN is equal to the angle LKN (1.4), that is, angle KAN = angle AKN.

**Step 11.** Since arc AK = arc KB (Step 4), the chord AK is equal to the chord KB (3.29); therefore in the triangle AKB the angle KAB is equal to the angle KBA (1.5). But angle KAB is the same as angle KAN, since N lies on AB; therefore angle AKN = angle KAN = angle KBA, that is, angle AKN = angle ABK (CN1).

**Step 12.** In the triangles AKN, ABK the angle at A is common, and the angle AKN is equal to the angle ABK; therefore the remaining angle ANK is equal to the remaining angle AKB (1.32), and the triangles are equiangular. Hence BA : AK = AK : AN (6.4), and the rectangle contained by BA, AN is equal to the square on AK (6.17).

**Step 13.** Since the straight line AB is cut at N, the rectangles contained by AB, AN and by AB, BN are together equal to the square on AB (2.2). But the rectangle AB, BN is equal to the square on BF (Step 9) and the rectangle BA, AN is equal to the square on AK (Step 12); therefore the square on AB is equal to the squares on BF and AK together (CN2).

**Step 14.** Now AB is the side of the pentagon. BF, being a radius, is equal to the side of the hexagon inscribed in the circle (4.15, porism). And AK is the side of the decagon inscribed in the circle: the ten equal sides of that decagon cut off ten equal arcs (3.28) which together make up the whole circumference, so each is a tenth part of it and is equal to arc AK (Step 4), and equal arcs are subtended by equal straight lines (3.29). Therefore the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 3.1, P1, P2, 1.12, 3.28, D1.17, CN2, CN3, 3.3, D1.10, 1.4, 3.26, 6.33, 1.32, 1.5, CN1, 6.4, 6.17, 3.29, 2.2, 4.15

result.statement: If in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor.
result.proof:
**Statement:** If in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be a circle whose diameter is rational, and let the equilateral pentagon ABCDE be inscribed in it, so that AB = BC = CD = DE = EA. Take the centre F of the circle (3.1). Join AF and BF (P1) and produce them to meet the circumference again at G and H respectively (P2); AG and BH are then diameters (D1.17). Join AC and BD (P1). Since FA = FB = FG = FH, being radii (D1.15), BH is double of BF and AG is double of AF. Bisect AF, and bisect the half again (1.10), so obtaining a fourth part of AF; on FH cut off FK equal to this fourth part (1.3). Then FA = FB = 4FK, BK = BF + FK = 5FK, BH = 2BF = 8FK, and K lies between F and H.

**Step 2.** Since the diameter is rational, take the diameter BH as the rational straight line set out. FK measures BH (BH = 8FK), and likewise measures FA, FB and BK; so each of FK, FA, FB, BK is commensurable in length with BH (D10.1.1) and is therefore rational (D10.1.3). Further, KF being commensurable in length with BH, the square on KF has to the square on BH the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), so these squares are commensurable (10.6); hence the square on KF is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 3.** Since the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal, they cut off equal circumferences (3.28); so the arcs AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal. Hence the arc ABC (= arcs AB + BC) is equal to the arc AED (= arcs AE + ED) (CN2), and therefore the chord AC is equal to the chord AD (3.29). Again, the angle EAB stands on the arc BCDE, the angle ABC on the arc CDEA, and similarly for the other angles; each of these arcs is made up of three of the five equal arcs, so they are all equal (CN2), and hence the five angles of the pentagon are equal (3.27). Thus the pentagon ABCDE is both equilateral and equiangular.

**Step 4.** In the triangles ABF, CBF, AB = CB, BF is common, and FA = FC (D1.15); therefore the angle ABF is equal to the angle CBF (1.8). So BF lies within the angle ABC and meets AC; let it meet AC at M. (M lies between B and F, because the arc ABC, being two of the five equal arcs, is less than a semicircle, so that the centre F lies on the side of AC remote from B.) In the triangles ABM, CBM, AB = CB, BM is common, and the angle ABM is equal to the angle CBM; therefore AM = MC and the angle AMB is equal to the angle CMB (1.4), so each of them is right (D1.10). Thus CA = 2CM, and CM is perpendicular to BH at M. On the line BH the points lie in the order B, M, F, K, H; hence BK = BM + MK and MK = MF + FK.

**Step 5.** In the triangles CAF, DAF, CA = DA (Step 3), AF is common, and FC = FD (D1.15); therefore the angle CAF is equal to the angle DAF (1.8). So AF produced, that is AG, lies within the angle CAD and meets CD; let it meet CD at L. In the triangles CAL, DAL, CA = DA, AL is common, and the angle CAL is equal to the angle DAL; therefore CL = LD and the angle ALC is equal to the angle ALD (1.4), so each of them is right (D1.10). Thus DC = 2CL.

**Step 6.** Consider the triangles ACL, AFM. The angle ALC is equal to the angle AMF, both being right (P4); and the angle CAL is the same angle as the angle FAM, since L lies on AF produced and M lies on AC. Therefore the remaining angle ACL is equal to the remaining angle AFM (1.32), and the triangles ACL, AFM are equiangular. Hence the sides about the equal angles are proportional, those sides corresponding which subtend equal angles (6.4): as CL is to CA, so is FM to FA (CA and FA subtending the right angles, CL and FM subtending the equal angles at A).

**Step 7.** Alternately (5.16), CL : FM = CA : FA. Now CL : FM = 2CL : 2FM = DC : 2FM (5.15, since DC = 2CL); and CA : FA = 2CM : 4FK = CM : 2FK (5.15, since CA = 2CM and FA = 4FK). Therefore DC : 2FM = CM : 2FK (5.11). Alternately (5.16), DC : CM = 2FM : 2FK; and 2FM : 2FK = FM : FK (5.15). Therefore DC : CM = FM : FK (5.11).

**Step 8.** Componendo (5.18), (DC + CM) : CM = (FM + FK) : FK, that is, (DC + CM) : CM = MK : KF, since MK = MF + FK (Step 4). The squares on these four straight lines being similar figures similarly described on them, the square on (DC + CM) is to the square on CM as the square on MK is to the square on KF (6.22).

**Step 9.** Since ABCDE is an equilateral and equiangular pentagon (Step 3), and the straight lines AC, BD subtend the two angles ABC, BCD taken in order, AC and BD cut one another in extreme and mean ratio, and the greater segment of each is equal to the side of the pentagon (13.8). Thus AC is cut in extreme and mean ratio, and its greater segment is equal to the side DC. Therefore the square on the greater segment together with the half of the whole AC, that is, the square on (DC + CM), CM being half of AC, is five times the square on the half CM (13.1): sq(DC + CM) = 5·sq(CM).

**Step 10.** From Steps 8 and 9, sq(MK) : sq(KF) = 5·sq(CM) : sq(CM). Alternately (5.16), sq(MK) : 5·sq(CM) = sq(KF) : sq(CM); and sq(KF) : sq(CM) = 5·sq(KF) : 5·sq(CM) (5.15); therefore sq(MK) : 5·sq(CM) = 5·sq(KF) : 5·sq(CM) (5.11), whence sq(MK) = 5·sq(KF) (5.9).

**Step 11.** Since sq(MK) is five times sq(KF), sq(MK) has to sq(KF) the ratio which the number five has to the unit; therefore sq(MK) is commensurable with sq(KF) (10.6). But sq(KF) is commensurable with sq(BH) (Step 2); therefore sq(MK) is commensurable with sq(BH) (10.12), so that sq(MK) is rational (D10.1.4), MK is commensurable in square with BH (D10.1.2), and MK is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 12.** Since BK = 5FK, BK has to KF the ratio 5 : 1; the square on BK has to the square on KF the ratio duplicate of this (6.20), namely 25 : 1 (D5.9), so sq(BK) = 25·sq(KF). But sq(MK) = 5·sq(KF) (Step 10); therefore sq(BK) = 5·sq(MK). Hence sq(BK) has to sq(MK) the ratio which the number five has to the unit, so sq(BK) and sq(MK) are commensurable (10.6), i.e. BK and MK are commensurable in square (D10.1.2); but five has not to one the ratio which a square number has to a square number, so BK is incommensurable in length with MK (10.9). Both BK (Step 2) and MK (Step 11) are rational; therefore BK, MK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Also BK is greater than MK, MK being a part of BK (CN5).

**Step 13.** Therefore BM, the remainder when the rational straight line MK, commensurable in square only with the whole BK, is subtracted from the rational straight line BK, is an apotome (10.73), BK being its whole and MK its annex.

**Step 14.** Now sq(BK) − sq(MK) = 5·sq(MK) − sq(MK) = 4·sq(MK). This is the square on the double of MK, since the square on the double of MK has to the square on MK the ratio duplicate of 2 : 1 (6.20), namely 4 : 1 (D5.9). And the square on the double of MK has to sq(BK) the ratio 4·sq(MK) : 5·sq(MK), that is 4 : 5, which is not the ratio of a square number to a square number; hence the double of MK is incommensurable in length with BK (10.9). Thus the square on the whole BK is greater than the square on the annex MK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BK, and the whole BK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line BH set out (Step 2). Therefore BM is a fourth apotome (D10.3.4).

**Step 15.** Join CH (P1). Since BH is a diameter, the angle BCH, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31). In the right-angled triangle BCH the perpendicular CM has been drawn from the right angle C to the base BH (Step 4), M lying between B and H; therefore BC is a mean proportional between the base BH and the segment BM adjacent to it (6.8): as BH is to BC, so is BC to BM. Hence the rectangle contained by BH, BM is equal to the square on BC (6.17).

**Step 16.** Thus the square on BC is equal to an area contained by the rational straight line BH and the fourth apotome BM. Therefore the "side" of this area, namely BC, is the irrational straight line called minor (10.94). And BC is the side of the pentagon. Therefore, if in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If an equilateral triangle be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the triangle is triple of the square on the radius of the circle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be the equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle ABC, so that AB = BC = CA (D1.20) and the points A, B, C lie on the circumference (D4.3). Take the centre D of the circle (3.1); join AD (P1) and produce it to meet the circumference again at E (P2); join DB and BE (P1). Since AE passes through the centre and is terminated in both directions by the circumference, AE is a diameter (D1.17), and the radii DA, DB, DE are equal to one another (D1.15).

**Step 2.** Since AB = AC, the angle ABC equals the angle ACB (1.5); and since BA = BC, the angle BAC equals the angle BCA (1.5). Hence the three angles of the triangle ABC are equal to one another (CN1). But the three angles of a triangle together equal two right angles (1.32); therefore two right angles equal three times the angle ACB.

**Step 3.** The angle ADB at the centre and the angle ACB at the circumference stand on the same circumference AB as base; therefore the angle ADB is double of the angle ACB (3.20).

**Step 4.** Since the straight line DB stands on the straight line AE at D, the adjacent angles ADB, BDE together equal two right angles (1.13). By Step 2 two right angles equal three times the angle ACB, and by Step 3 the angle ADB equals twice the angle ACB; taking away the angle ADB, the remaining angle BDE equals the angle ACB (CN3).

**Step 5.** In the triangle DBE, DB = DE (Step 1); therefore the angle DBE equals the angle DEB (1.5). The three angles of the triangle DBE together equal two right angles (1.32), that is, three times the angle ACB (Step 2). Taking away the angle BDE, which equals the angle ACB (Step 4), the remaining angles DBE, DEB together equal twice the angle ACB (CN3); and since they are equal to one another, each of them equals the angle ACB. Therefore the angle DBE equals the angle BDE (CN1), and the sides subtending these equal angles are equal: DE = BE (1.6).

**Step 6.** Since AE is a diameter, the angle ABE in the semicircle ABE is a right angle (3.31). Hence in the right-angled triangle ABE the square on AE equals the squares on AB, BE (1.47).

**Step 7.** The straight line AE is cut at D into the parts AD, DE; therefore the square on AE equals the squares on AD, DE together with twice the rectangle contained by AD, DE (2.4). Since AD = DE, each of the squares on AD, DE and the rectangle AD, DE is equal to the square on DE; therefore the square on AE is four times the square on DE.

**Step 8.** From Step 6, the square on AB equals the square on AE less the square on BE (CN3). The square on AE is four times the square on DE (Step 7), and the square on BE equals the square on DE, since BE = DE (Step 5). Therefore the square on AB equals four times the square on DE less the square on DE, that is, three times the square on DE. Hence the square on the side AB of the triangle is triple of the square on the radius DE of the circle. Q.E.D.

Path note: an equivalent route establishes BE = DE by showing that the circumference BE is a sixth part of the whole (3.28) so that BE is the side of the inscribed hexagon (4.15 Por.); the angle-at-the-centre route (3.20, 1.13, 1.6) was chosen because it reaches BE = DE without reasoning about fractions of the circumference or the position of E on the arc BC.

result.statement: To construct a pyramid, to comprehend it in a given sphere, and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a diameter of the given sphere (D11.17). Cut off from AB its third part CB (6.9); then AC is double of CB, and AB, being AC together with CB, is triple of CB (CN2).

**Step 2.** Bisect AB at O (1.10), and with centre O and distance OA describe the semicircle ADB on AB (P3). From the point C draw CD at right angles to AB (1.11), meeting the circumference at D, and join DA, DB (P1).

**Step 3.** The angle ADB is an angle in a semicircle, so it is right (3.31). In the right-angled triangle ADB the perpendicular DC has been drawn from the right angle to the base AB; hence the triangles ADC, DBC are similar to the whole triangle ADB and to one another (6.8), and the sides about their equal angles are proportional (6.4): BA : AD = AD : AC, and AC : CD = CD : CB. Therefore the square on AD is equal to the rectangle BA, AC, and the square on CD is equal to the rectangle AC, CB (6.17).

**Step 4.** The rectangles BA, AC and AC, CB stand under the same height AC, so they are to one another as their bases (6.1): rectangle BA, AC : rectangle AC, CB = BA : CB. Hence, by Step 3, the square on AD : the square on CD = AB : CB. But AB is triple of CB (Step 1); therefore the square on AD is triple of the square on CD.

**Step 5.** Take a point H in any plane, and with centre H and distance equal to CD describe the circle EFG (P3). Construct an equilateral triangle (1.1); its three angles are equal to one another (1.5). In the circle EFG inscribe a triangle EFG equiangular with it (4.2); having its three angles equal, it has its three sides equal (1.6), so EFG is an equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle. Join HE, HF, HG (P1). These are radii of the circle, so HE = HF = HG = CD (D1.15).

**Step 6.** Since the equilateral triangle EFG is inscribed in the circle whose radius is HE, the square on EF is triple of the square on EH (13.12), that is, triple of the square on CD. But the square on AD is also triple of the square on CD (Step 4). Therefore the square on AD is equal to the square on EF (CN1), and AD = EF.

**Step 7.** From H set up HK at right angles to the plane of the circle EFG (11.12), cut off HK equal to AC (1.3), and join KE, KF, KG (P1). Since KH is at right angles to the plane, it makes right angles with HE, HF, HG, which meet it and lie in that plane (D11.3): the angles KHE, KHF, KHG are right.

**Step 8.** In the triangles KHE, ACD the two sides KH, HE are equal to the two sides AC, CD respectively, and the included angles KHE, ACD are equal, both being right (P4); therefore the base KE is equal to the base AD (1.4). In the same way KF = AD and KG = AD. Hence KE = KF = KG = AD = EF = FG = GE (CN1, Step 6). Thus the solid figure constructed from the base EFG to the point K, which is a pyramid (D11.12), is contained by the four equilateral triangles EFG, KEF, KFG, KGE. A pyramid has been constructed.

**Step 9.** Produce KH beyond H to L (P2), cut off HL equal to CB (1.3), and bisect KL at M (1.10). Then KL, being KH together with HL, is equal to AC together with CB, that is, to AB (CN2).

**Step 10.** Since KH = AC, HL = CB and HE = CD, the rectangle KH, HL is equal to the rectangle AC, CB, which is equal to the square on CD (Step 3); hence the rectangle KH, HL is equal to the square on HE.

**Step 11.** The straight line KL is cut into equal segments at M and into unequal segments at H; therefore the rectangle KH, HL together with the square on HM is equal to the square on KM (2.5). By Step 10, the square on HE together with the square on HM is equal to the square on KM.

**Step 12.** Since the angle KHE is right (Step 7), the adjacent angle EHL is also right (1.13); so HE is at right angles to the whole line KL, and, M lying on KL, the angle EHM is right. Join EM (P1). In the right-angled triangle EHM the square on EM is equal to the squares on EH, HM (1.47), which together are equal to the square on KM (Step 11). Therefore EM = KM.

**Step 13.** Join FM, GM (P1). In the triangles EHM, FHM the two sides EH, HM are equal to the two sides FH, HM (Step 5), and the included angles EHM, FHM are right and therefore equal (P4); so FM = EM (1.4). Likewise GM = EM. Hence MK, ML, ME, MF, MG are all equal to one another (CN1).

**Step 14.** With centre M and distance MK describe a semicircle on KL (P3), and let it be carried round about the fixed diameter KL and restored to the position from which it began to move; the figure so comprehended is a sphere whose diameter is KL (D11.14, D11.17). When the semicircle comes into the plane through KL and E, its circumference passes through E, because ME is equal to the radius MK (D1.15); in the same way it passes through F and through G. Thus the four vertices K, E, F, G of the pyramid lie on the surface of this sphere, and the pyramid is comprehended in it. Since KL = AB (Step 9), this sphere has its diameter equal to the diameter of the given sphere and is therefore equal to it; so the pyramid has been comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 15.** The square on AB and the rectangle AB, AC stand under the same height AB, so the square on AB : the rectangle AB, AC = AB : AC (6.1). But the rectangle AB, AC is equal to the square on AD (Step 3), which is equal to the square on EF (Step 6). Therefore the square on AB : the square on EF = AB : AC.

**Step 16.** AB is triple of CB and AC is double of CB (Step 1), so AB exceeds AC by CB, which is the half of AC; that is, AB is one and a half times AC. Therefore the square on AB is one and a half times the square on EF. Since AB is the diameter of the sphere and EF is the side of the pyramid, the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To construct an octahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, as in the preceding case; and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is double of the square on the side of the octahedron.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a diameter of the given sphere [D11.17]. Bisect AB at C [1.10]. On AB describe the semicircle ADB [P3, D1.18]; from C draw CD at right angles to AB [1.11], meeting the semicircle at D; and join DB [P1].

**Step 2.** Take a straight line EF equal to DB [1.3] and on EF describe the square EFGH [1.46]. Join HF and EG [P1], and let them cut one another at K. From K set up KL at right angles to the plane of EFGH [11.12], and produce LK through the plane to the other side, to M [P2]. From the two sides cut off KL and KM each equal to EK [1.3]. Join LE, LF, LG, LH, ME, MF, MG, MH [P1].

**Step 3.** Since EFGH is a square, its four sides are equal and its four angles are right [D1.22]. In triangle HEF, EH = EF, so angle EHF = angle EFH [1.5]; the three angles of triangle HEF together equal two right angles [1.32], and angle HEF is right, so angles EHF, EFH together equal one right angle, and each of them is half a right angle. In the same way, from triangle EHG (HE = HG, angle EHG right) each of the angles HEG, HGE is half a right angle; from triangle FGH (GF = GH, angle FGH right) each of GFH, GHF is half a right angle; and from triangle EFG (FE = FG, angle EFG right) each of FEG, FGE is half a right angle. Thus each of the eight angles which the diagonals HF, EG make with the sides at E, F, G, H is half a right angle.

**Step 4.** In triangle EKH, angle KEH = angle KHE, each being half a right angle; therefore KE = KH [1.6]. And since the three angles of triangle EKH equal two right angles [1.32] and the two angles at E and H together make one right angle, angle EKH is a right angle. In the same way, from triangles EKF, FKG, GKH: KE = KF, KF = KG, KG = KH, and the angles EKF, FKG, GKH are right. Therefore KE = KF = KG = KH [CN1], and the four angles at K are all right.

**Step 5.** Since angle EKH is right, the square on EH equals the squares on EK, KH [1.47]; and KH = KE, so the square on EH is double the square on EK. Likewise each of the squares on EF, FG, GH is double the square on EK.

**Step 6.** Since the straight line LM stands at right angles to the plane of EFGH, it makes right angles with every straight line in that plane which meets it [D11.3]; therefore the angles LKE, LKF, LKG, LKH, MKE, MKF, MKG, MKH are all right. In triangle LKE the square on LE equals the squares on LK, KE [1.47]; and LK = KE, so the square on LE is double the square on KE.

**Step 7.** But the square on EH is also double the square on EK (Step 5); therefore the square on LE equals the square on EH [CN1], and so LE = EH. In the same way, since each of LK, MK equals each of KE, KF, KG, KH, and every angle at K is right, each of LF, LG, LH, ME, MF, MG, MH is equal to a side of the square, that is, to EH.

**Step 8.** Therefore each of the eight triangles LEF, LFG, LGH, LHE, MEF, MFG, MGH, MHE has its three sides equal to EH and is equilateral [D1.20]; and, having their sides respectively equal, they have their angles respectively equal [1.8] and are equal to one another [1.4]. The four triangles with vertex L and the four with vertex M stand on the same square EFGH on opposite sides of its plane, so together they contain a solid figure bounded by eight equal and equilateral triangles: an octahedron has been constructed [D11.26].

**Step 9.** Since KL = KM = KE, the circle described in the plane of L, M, E with centre K and distance KL [P3] passes through E [D1.15], and LM, passing through the centre K, is a diameter of it [D1.17]; so LEM is a semicircle on LM [D1.18]. Let the diameter LM remain fixed and the semicircle LEM be carried round and restored to the position from which it began to be moved: the figure comprehended is a sphere [D11.14] whose diameter is LM [D11.17]. When the turning semicircle comes into the plane of L, M, F it is the semicircle on LM with centre K and distance KL in that plane, and since KF = KL it passes through F [D1.15]; similarly it passes through G and through H. Thus the surface of this sphere passes through all six vertices L, M, E, F, G, H, and the octahedron is comprehended in the sphere.

**Step 10.** The angle LEM is in the semicircle LEM, so it is right [3.31]. Hence the square on LM equals the squares on LE, EM [1.47]; and LE = EM, each being equal to EH (Step 7); therefore the square on LM is double the square on LE.

**Step 11.** In triangles ACD, BCD: AC = CB, CD is common, and the angles ACD, BCD are right; therefore AD = DB [1.4]. The angle ADB is in the semicircle ADB, so it is right [3.31]. Hence the square on AB equals the squares on AD, DB [1.47], that is, the square on AB is double the square on DB. (Path note: this direct route through 1.4 and 1.47 is chosen over the proportional route that treats DB as the mean proportional between AB and BC, since it reaches the doubling in fewer steps.)

**Step 12.** Now EH was made equal to DB, and LE = EH (Step 7); therefore LE = DB [CN1], and the square on LE equals the square on DB. So the square on LM, which is double the square on LE, equals the square on AB, which is double the square on DB [CN1]; hence LM = AB.

**Step 13.** But AB is the diameter of the given sphere; therefore LM, the diameter of the sphere in which the octahedron is comprehended, equals the diameter of the given sphere, and that sphere is the given sphere. Therefore the octahedron has been comprehended in the given sphere; and since the square on AB equals the square on LM, which is double the square on LE, the square on the diameter of the sphere is double the square on the side of the octahedron. Q.E.D.
