result.statement: To construct a cube and comprehend it in a sphere, like the pyramid; and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the diameter of the given sphere. Cut off from AB a third part CB [6.9]; then AB is triple of CB, and the remainder AC is double of CB.

**Step 2.** Bisect AB at O [1.10]; with centre O and distance OA describe a circle [P3]; the part of it on one side of the diameter AB is the semicircle ADB [D1.18]. From C draw CD at right angles to AB [1.11], meeting the circumference at D, and join DB [P1].

**Step 3.** The angle ADB, being an angle in the semicircle ADB, is right [3.31]. Thus ADB is a right-angled triangle, and DC is the perpendicular drawn from the right angle to the base AB; therefore the triangle DBC is similar to the whole triangle ABD, and, the sides about the common angle at B being proportional, AB : BD = BD : BC [6.8].

**Step 4.** Since AB, BD, BC are three proportional straight lines, AB has to BC the ratio duplicate of that which AB has to BD [D5.9]. But the square on AB has to the square on BD the ratio duplicate of that which AB has to BD, the two squares being similar rectilineal figures [6.20]. Therefore, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the square on BD [5.11]. And AB is triple of BC (Step 1); therefore the square on AB is triple of the square on BD [D5.5].

**Step 5.** Let a straight line EF be taken equal to DB [1.3], and on EF let the square EFGH be described [1.46]. From the points E, F, G, H let EK, FL, GM, HN be set up at right angles to the plane of the square EFGH [11.12], and let EK, FL, GM, HN be cut off each equal to EF [1.3]. Join KL, LM, MN, NK [P1].

**Step 6.** Since EK and FL are both at right angles to the same plane EFGH, EK is parallel to FL [11.6]; hence E, F, L, K lie in one plane [D1.23]. Moreover EK = FL, and KL joins their extremities in the same direction; therefore KL is equal and parallel to EF [1.33]. In the same way FL is parallel to GM, GM to HN, and HN to EK [11.6], and LM is equal and parallel to FG, MN to GH, and NK to HE [1.33].

**Step 7.** In the plane quadrilateral EFLK the four sides EF, FL, LK, KE are all equal to EF (Steps 5, 6), so it is equilateral. Since EK is at right angles to the plane EFGH, it makes a right angle with EF, which lies in that plane [D11.3]; so the angle KEF is right, and likewise the angle EFL is right, FL being at right angles to the same plane [D11.3]. Since KL is parallel to EF and EK falls on them, the angles EKL, KEF together equal two right angles [1.29], so that the angle EKL is right; and since FL falls on the same parallels, the angle KLF is right likewise [1.29]. Therefore EFLK is equilateral and right-angled, that is, a square [D1.22], and it is equal to the square EFGH, its side being equal to EF. In the same way FGML, GHNM, HEKN are squares equal to EFGH.

**Step 8.** KL is parallel to EF and MN to GH (Step 6), and EF is parallel to GH, because the angles EFG, FGH of the square are together equal to two right angles [1.28]; these straight lines not being all in one plane, KL is parallel to GH, and hence KL is parallel to MN [11.9]. Therefore K, L, M, N lie in one plane [D1.23]. The sides KL, LM, MN, NK are equal to EF, FG, GH, HE respectively (Step 6), hence all equal, so KLMN is equilateral. Again, LK, LM meeting at L are parallel respectively to FE, FG meeting at F, and the two pairs are not in the same plane; therefore the angle KLM is equal to the angle EFG [11.10], which is right. Similarly the angles LMN, MNK, NKL are right. Hence KLMN is a square [D1.22] equal to EFGH.

**Step 9.** Therefore the solid figure bounded by EFGH, KLMN, EFLK, FGML, GHNM, HEKN is contained by six equal squares, and so it is a cube [D11.25]; its side EF is equal to DB.

**Step 10.** Join KG and EG [P1]. Since KE is at right angles to the plane EFGH and EG lies in that plane, the angle KEG is right [D11.3]. Therefore the semicircle described on KG in the plane of K, E, G passes through E; for the angle in a semicircle is right [3.31].

**Step 11.** Again, GF is at right angles to FE, the angle EFG of the square being right, and also to FL, since FL is at right angles to the plane EFGH in which GF lies [D11.3]; and FE, FL cut one another at F. Therefore GF is at right angles to the plane through FE, FL, that is, the plane of the square EFLK [11.4]. Join FK [P1]; FK, joining points on the parallels EK, FL, lies in that plane [11.7]; therefore GF is at right angles to FK [D11.3], and the angle KFG is right. Hence the semicircle described on KG in the plane of K, F, G passes through F [3.31].

**Step 12.** In the same way GH, being at right angles to HE and to HN, is at right angles to the plane of the square HEKN [11.4], in which HK lies [11.7], so that the angle KHG is right. KL, being at right angles to LF and to LM (Steps 7, 8), is at right angles to the plane of the square FGML [11.4], in which LG lies [11.7], so that the angle KLG is right; likewise KN is at right angles to the plane of the square GHNM, in which NG lies, so that the angle KNG is right. Lastly, since EK and GM are equal and parallel, KM is equal and parallel to EG [1.33]; GM makes a right angle with GE, which lies in the plane EFGH [D11.3]; and since KM is parallel to EG and GM falls on them, the angles KMG, MGE together equal two right angles [1.29], so that the angle KMG is right. Therefore the semicircles described on KG in the planes of KHG, KLG, KNG, KMG pass through H, L, N, M respectively [3.31].

**Step 13.** If then, KG remaining fixed, the semicircle described on KG be carried round and restored to the same position from which it began to be moved, the figure so comprehended is a sphere [D11.14], of which KG is a diameter [D11.17]. In its revolution the semicircle passes through each of the points E, F, H, L, M, N (Steps 10-12), while K and G are the extremities of the diameter; hence all eight angular points of the cube lie on the surface of this sphere, and the cube is comprehended in it.

**Step 14.** Since the angle EFG is right, the square on EG is equal to the squares on EF, FG [1.47], that is, to double the square on EF, because FG is equal to EF. And since the angle KEG is right (Step 10), the square on KG is equal to the squares on KE, EG [1.47]; and KE is equal to EF; therefore the square on KG is triple of the square on EF.

**Step 15.** But EF is equal to DB (Step 5), so that the square on EF is equal to the square on DB; therefore the square on KG is triple of the square on DB. And the square on AB is triple of the square on DB (Step 4). Therefore the square on KG is equal to the square on AB [CN1], and KG is equal to AB. Thus the diameter KG of the sphere comprehending the cube is equal to the diameter AB of the given sphere, so that this sphere is equal to the given sphere; therefore the cube has been comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 16.** Finally, the square on AB, the diameter of the sphere, is equal to the square on KG, which is triple of the square on EF, the side of the cube (Step 14). Therefore a cube has been constructed and comprehended in the given sphere, and the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To construct an icosahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures; and to prove that the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the diameter of the given sphere, and let AB be taken as the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.3), to which the irrationality of the side will be referred. From AB cut off a fifth part CB (6.9), so that AC is four times CB and AB is five times CB. Bisect AB (1.10), and with that midpoint as centre and half AB as distance describe the semicircle ADB on AB (P3, D1.18). At C draw CD at right angles to AB (1.11), meeting the semicircle at D, and join DB (P1).

**Step 2.** The angle ADB, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31). In the right-angled triangle ADB the perpendicular DC has been drawn from the right angle to the base AB, so the triangle DBC is similar to the triangle ABD (6.8); hence the sides about the common angle at B are proportional, AB : BD = BD : BC (D6.1), and therefore the rectangle AB, BC is equal to the square on BD (6.17). Now AB is made up of five segments each equal to BC, so the rectangle AB, AB, that is the square on AB, is equal to five rectangles AB, BC (2.1). Therefore the square on AB is five times the square on BD.

**Step 3.** Take a point V, and with centre V and distance equal to DB describe the circle EFGHK (P3); VE, VF, VG, VH, VK are its radii, each equal to DB. In it inscribe the equilateral and equiangular pentagon EFGHK (4.11). Since the chords EF, FG, GH, HK, KE are equal, the arcs EF, FG, GH, HK, KE which they cut off are equal (3.28). Bisect these arcs at L, M, N, O, P respectively (3.30), and join LM, MN, NO, OP, PL and EL, LF, FM, MG, GN, NH, HO, OK, KP, PE (P1).

**Step 4.** The ten arcs EL, LF, FM, MG, GN, NH, HO, OK, KP, PE are halves of the five equal arcs, hence are all equal to one another; therefore the ten chords EL, LF, FM, MG, GN, NH, HO, OK, KP, PE are equal (3.29), so that ELFMGNHOKP is an equilateral decagon inscribed in the circle, and each of these chords is the side of the decagon inscribed in the circle EFGHK. Further, the arc LM is made up of the arcs LF, FM, which are equal respectively to the arcs EL, LF making up the arc EF; hence the arc LM equals the arc EF, and the chord LM equals the chord EF (3.29). Similarly MN, NO, OP, PL each equal EF; thus LMNOP is an equilateral pentagon inscribed in the circle, with side equal to EF. Also the radius VE of the circle is equal to the side of the hexagon inscribed in it (4.15).

**Step 5.** Since the equilateral pentagon EFGHK is inscribed in the circle, the square on its side EF is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on the side of the decagon inscribed in the same circle (13.10); that is, the square on EF is equal to the squares on VE and EL together, where VE is the radius and EL is the side of the decagon.

**Step 6.** From the points E, F, G, H, K set up EQ, FR, GS, HT, KU at right angles to the plane of the circle EFGHK (11.12), all on the same side of the plane, and cut off each of them equal to the radius VE (1.3). Join QR, RS, ST, TU, UQ, and QL, LR, RM, MS, SN, NT, TO, OU, UP, PQ (P1).

**Step 7.** Since EQ and FR are at right angles to the same plane, they are parallel (11.6); and they are equal. Therefore QR, joining their extremities in the same directions, is equal and parallel to EF (1.33). Similarly RS = FG, ST = GH, TU = HK, UQ = KE. Hence each of QR, RS, ST, TU, UQ is equal to EF.

**Step 8.** Since EQ is at right angles to the plane of the circle, it makes right angles with EL, which lies in that plane and meets it (D11.3); so the angle QEL is right, and the square on QL is equal to the squares on QE and EL (1.47). But QE equals the radius VE, and EL is the side of the decagon; therefore the square on QL is equal to the square on EF (Step 5), and QL = EF. In the same way, since FL, FM, GM, GN, HN, HO, KO, KP, EP are each the side of the decagon, and FR, GS, HT, KU, EQ are each equal to the radius and at right angles to the plane, each of LR, RM, MS, SN, NT, TO, OU, UP, PQ is equal to EF.

**Step 9.** Therefore the ten triangles QLR, LRM, RMS, MSN, SNT, NTO, TOU, OUP, UPQ, PQL are equilateral, every side of each being equal to EF (Steps 4, 7, 8).

**Step 10.** From the centre V set up VZ at right angles to the plane of the circle (11.12), on the same side as EQ, and produce it through V to the other side of the plane (P2). On VZ cut off VW equal to the radius VE and WZ equal to EP, the side of the decagon, W lying between V and Z; and on the production cut off VX equal to EP (1.3). Join QZ, RZ, SZ, TZ, UZ, LX, MX, NX, OX, PX, and WQ, WR, WS, WT, WU (P1).

**Step 11.** Since VW and EQ are at right angles to the same plane, they are parallel (11.6); and they are equal, each being equal to VE. Therefore WQ, joining their extremities in the same directions, is equal and parallel to VE (1.33). Similarly WR = VF, WS = VG, WT = VH, WU = VK. Hence each of WQ, WR, WS, WT, WU is equal to the radius VE.

**Step 12.** Since VW is at right angles to the plane of the circle, the angle EVW is right (D11.3). Since WQ is parallel to VE and VW falls on them, the interior angles QWV, EVW on the same side are together equal to two right angles (1.29); hence the angle QWV is right. Then the angles QWV, QWZ, being adjacent angles on the straight line VZ, are together equal to two right angles (1.13); hence the angle QWZ is right. Therefore the square on QZ is equal to the squares on QW and WZ (1.47), that is, to the squares on the radius VE and on the side EP of the decagon, that is, to the square on EF (Step 5); so QZ = EF. Similarly RZ, SZ, TZ, UZ are each equal to EF. Therefore the five triangles QRZ, RSZ, STZ, TUZ, UQZ are equilateral, with every side equal to EF (Step 7).

**Step 13.** Since VZ is at right angles to the plane of the circle, the angle ZVL is right (D11.3), and hence its adjacent angle XVL on the straight line ZX is also right (1.13). Therefore the square on LX is equal to the squares on LV and VX (1.47), that is, to the squares on the radius and on the side of the decagon, that is, to the square on EF (Step 5); so LX = EF. Similarly MX, NX, OX, PX are each equal to EF. Therefore the five triangles LMX, MNX, NOX, OPX, PLX are equilateral, with every side equal to EF (Step 4).

**Step 14.** Hence a solid figure has been constructed which is contained by the twenty triangles of Steps 9, 12 and 13, namely the ten triangles QLR, LRM, RMS, MSN, SNT, NTO, TOU, OUP, UPQ, PQL, the five triangles QRZ, RSZ, STZ, TUZ, UQZ, and the five triangles LMX, MNX, NOX, OPX, PLX. Each of these is equilateral and all their sides are equal to EF, so they are twenty equal and equilateral triangles; therefore the solid is an icosahedron (D11.27), and its side is equal to EF, the side of the pentagon inscribed in the circle EFGHK.

**Step 15.** Next, it is to be comprehended in a sphere. Since VW is the side of the hexagon and WZ the side of the decagon inscribed in the same circle EFGHK, and VZ is made up of them, VZ has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at W, and VW is its greater segment (13.9). Bisect VW at Y (1.10). Then, VZ being cut in extreme and mean ratio at W, the square on the lesser segment ZW added to the half WY of the greater segment, that is, the square on ZY, is five times the square on WY (13.3).

**Step 16.** Since VW is bisected at Y, the square on VW is four times the square on WY (2.4). The angle QWY is right, being the angle QWV (Step 12). Therefore the square on QY is equal to the squares on QW and WY (1.47); and QW equals VE, which equals VW; so the square on QY is equal to four times the square on WY together with the square on WY, that is, to five times the square on WY, that is, to the square on ZY (Step 15). Hence QY = ZY. Similarly RY, SY, TY, UY are each equal to ZY.

**Step 17.** Since XV = WZ, each being equal to EP, and VY = YW, the whole XY is equal to the whole ZY (CN2). Again, since VZ is at right angles to the plane of the circle, the angle LVY is right (D11.3); therefore the square on LY is equal to the squares on LV and VY (1.47). And LV is the radius, equal to VW, whose square is four times the square on VY (2.4); so the square on LY is five times the square on VY, that is, five times the square on WY, that is, the square on ZY (Step 15). Hence LY = ZY. Similarly MY, NY, OY, PY are each equal to ZY.

**Step 18.** Therefore the straight lines drawn from Y to all twelve vertices Q, R, S, T, U, L, M, N, O, P, X, Z are equal to YZ (Steps 16, 17). Describe on XZ the semicircle with centre Y and distance YZ (P3, D1.18), and let it be carried round about XZ, which remains fixed, until it is restored to the position from which it began to be moved; the figure so comprehended is a sphere (D11.14), of which XZ is a diameter and Y the centre (D11.17, D11.16). As the semicircle is carried round it passes through the plane containing XZ and any vertex, say Q; and in that plane, since YQ = YZ, the point Q lies on the circle with centre Y and distance YZ (D1.15), that is, on the surface of the sphere. The same holds for every vertex. Therefore the icosahedron has been comprehended in this sphere.

**Step 19.** This sphere is equal to the given sphere. For XZ is bisected at Y, so the square on XZ is four times the square on ZY (2.4), that is, four times five times the square on WY (Step 15), that is, five times four times the square on WY, that is, five times the square on VW (Step 16). But VW equals the radius VE, which equals DB; so the square on XZ is five times the square on DB, which is the square on AB (Step 2). Therefore XZ = AB, and the sphere on the diameter XZ is the given sphere. Thus the icosahedron has been constructed and comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 20.** Finally, the side of the icosahedron is minor. The diameter of the circle EFGHK is double the radius, that is, double DB, so its square is four times the square on DB (2.4). Since the square on AB is five times the square on DB (Step 2), five times the square on the diameter of the circle is twenty times the square on DB, which is four times the square on AB. Hence the square on the diameter of the circle has to the square on AB the ratio which the number 4 has to the number 5; therefore these squares are commensurable (10.6), so the diameter of the circle is commensurable in square with the rational straight line AB and is therefore itself rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 21.** Therefore the circle EFGHK has its diameter rational, and in it the equilateral pentagon EFGHK is inscribed; hence the side EF of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor (13.11). But every side of the icosahedron is equal to EF (Step 14). Therefore the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To construct a dodecahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Setting out. Let the diameter of the given sphere be taken as the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.3). By 13.15 construct a cube comprehended in this sphere; then the diameter of the cube is a diameter of the sphere and the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube (13.15). The square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side BC of the cube (13.15), so the square on BC has to the square on the diameter the ratio 1 : 3, which a number has to a number; hence these squares are commensurable (10.6). The square on the diameter is rational (D10.1.4), so BC is commensurable in square with the assigned rational line (D10.1.2) and is therefore rational (D10.1.3). NO = BC (Step 2), so NO is rational.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the diameter of the given sphere. Bisect AB at C [1.10], and cut off from AB its third part DB at D [6.9], so that AC = CB and AD = 2DB. With centre C and distance CA describe the semicircle AEB on AB [P3, D1.18]; C is its centre. From C and D draw CE and DF at right angles to AB [1.11], meeting the semicircle at E and F, and join AF, FB, EB [P1].

**Step 3.** The angle AFB is in a semicircle, hence right [3.31]; and FD is drawn from the right angle perpendicular to the base AB. Therefore the triangles AFD, FBD are each similar to the whole triangle AFB [6.8], and from the equiangular triangles AFB, ADF and AFB, FDB we have BA : AF = AF : AD and AB : BF = BF : BD [6.4].

**Step 4.** Since BA, AF, AD are three proportional straight lines, BA has to AD the ratio duplicate of that which BA has to AF [D5.9], and the square on BA has to the square on AF that same duplicate ratio [6.20 por.]; hence BA : AD = sq(BA) : sq(AF). But BA is one and a half times AD [Step 2]; therefore sq(AB) is one and a half times sq(AF). Now the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid inscribed in that sphere [13.13]; therefore sq(AF) equals the square on the side of the pyramid, and AF is the side of the pyramid.

**Step 5.** Likewise, from AB : BF = BF : BD we get AB : BD = sq(AB) : sq(BF) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]; and AB = 3BD [Step 2], so sq(AB) = 3 sq(BF). The square on the diameter of the sphere is triple the square on the side of the cube inscribed in it [13.15]; therefore BF is the side of the cube.

**Step 6.** The angle AEB is right [3.31], and EC is the perpendicular from it to AB; so the triangles AEC, EBC are similar to AEB [6.8], whence AB : BE = BE : BC [6.4], and AB : BC = sq(AB) : sq(BE) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. Since AB = 2BC [Step 2], sq(AB) = 2 sq(BE). The square on the diameter of the sphere is double the square on the side of the octahedron inscribed in it [13.14]; therefore BE is the side of the octahedron.

**Step 7.** For the icosahedron: at A draw AG at right angles to AB [1.11], make AG = AB [1.3], and join GC [P1]. In triangle GAC the angle at A is right, so sq(CG) = sq(CA) + sq(AG) [1.47], which is greater than sq(CA) [CN5]; thus CG > CA, the radius, and G lies outside the circle. Since C is the centre, GC cuts the semicircle at a point H between G and C. From H draw HK perpendicular to AB [1.12]; K falls between A and C.

AB is that diameter; hence sq(KL) equals the square on that radius, and KL equals that radius, that is, KL is the side of the hexagon inscribed in that circle [4.15 por.].
